risks: Low: the project changes who removes catheters and when. The main risks are unsafe removal leading to retention and reinsertion, and staff feeling blamed for catheters left in; results are reported by ward, never by nurse.
consent: Standard work is usual care under an approved nurse-driven protocol; patients are told why their catheter is being removed and can ask to keep it pending review. Staff take part as part of normal work.
data: Ward-level counts only leave each hospital; patient identifiers stay in the local surveillance system; Hospital D's data are shared only after its information governance office agrees.
equity: PROGRESS-Plus: older men after surgery bear most reinsertion risk, patients with dementia or limited English may not report retention symptoms, and night-shift wards have fewer staff to act on reminders. Reinsertion is reported by age group, bladder scanning is used before reinsertion, and interpreters are used for removal explanations.
effectiveness: Success is a sustained fall in catheter days with reinsertion below 6 percent; infections are described, never claimed as an effect.
efficiency: Existing staff, one coach and existing data systems.
costs: Staff time within normal work; bladder scanners already on the wards.
grants: None needed; a regional spread grant could follow.
partnerships: Four ward manager champions, the regional Lean office, urology and emergency leads, and two patient partners from the regional advisory council.
rebPath: Screened by the regional research ethics office as quality improvement not requiring REB review (QI-R-2026-077); any later publication follows SQUIRE 2.0.
limitations: Non-randomised; infections too few to test; surveillance intensity may change.
summary: Low-risk improvement work under a QI screening, with ward-level reporting and a data sharing condition for Hospital D.
